text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Apartment owners in Stockholm have been fooled to sell their flats cheaply to private persons working through a broker. The buyers have then immediately sold the apartments for a much higher price, according to a newspaper study.
- A company comittee proposed on Monday that Swedish corporations be allowed to buy back their own shares of up to ten percent of equity.

- The number of newly registered cars in Sweden rose strongly in the first two months of this year, according to industry group Bilindustriforeningen. In January and February 24 percent more cars were registered than in the same period a year ago.

- The Swedish union for people with a university education and white collar worker union TCO are on the verge of agreeing on how to deal with wage negotiations and wages in the future. A document, which will be presented to the government, is being discussed within TCO, while Saco already approved it. The proposal dismisses central wage negotiations and is positive to local solutions.
- A company comittee proposed on Monday that Swedish corporations be allowed to buy back their own shares, up to ten percent of equity, as of January 1, 1999.

- The Swedish economy is picking up, albeit slowly, according to two surveys published on Monday. The purchasing managers' index for February was well above the 50 point limit indicating growth, while Statistics Sweden's consumer confidence indicator survey showed households were less pessimistic.

- Suspicions of industrial espionage have arisen in the aftermath of Swedish company ID Kort Sakerhetstryck's unsuccessful attempt to win a national driver licence contract worth 420 million crowns in South Africa. The Swedish firm and local partners in Pretoria lost corporate information during a series of robberies in the months before the contract was awarded to another company. ID Kort sales director Christer Soderberg says the rival allegedly used his company's computer equipment in its presentation.

- Volvo Cars shaved 2.4 billion crowns off costs last year by reducing its workforce by 2,500 employees. This was substantially more than the total group profit of 1.5 billion crowns. Volvo says it expects to boost volumes in 1997.

- Swedish industrial gas producer AGA said 1996 profit before one-time gains fell a greater-than-expected 17 percent due to a stronger Swedish crown and weaker demand. Pre-tax profit and one-time gains totalled 1.75 billion crowns. The company itself had expected a 15 percent fall from 2.1 billion crowns in 1995.
